subject: English
description: Prepositions — time/place/movement; idiomatic prepositions; common errors with by/from/since/for/on/in/at; distinct senses.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I have been waiting ___ two hours.'
questions.explanation: FOR + DURATION (length of time); SINCE + STARTING POINT (specific time/date). 'Waiting FOR 2 hours' = duration. 'Waiting SINCE 9 AM' = starting point. EXAMPLES: (1) 'I have lived here for 5 years.' (2) 'I have lived here since 2020.' (3) 'I haven't seen her for 3 months.' (4) 'I haven't seen her since June.' KEY USAGE: FOR — duration: 'for an hour, for 2 days, for years'. SINCE — point in time: 'since Monday, since 1990, since I was a child, since lunch'. SAMPLE COMBINATIONS — 'I've been studying for 3 hours since 8 PM' (both used together). FROM — similar to 'since' for STARTING POINT but typically used with END point: 'from Monday TO Friday', 'from morning till night', 'from 9 to 5'. WHEN to use FROM vs SINCE: SINCE is for present-perfect tense + still ongoing; FROM is for an ENDED PERIOD. e.g., 'I worked there FROM 2018 TO 2022' (no longer there) vs 'I have worked there SINCE 2018' (still working). IN: typically with a complete period — 'in 2020, in March, in the morning'. AT: with specific times — 'at 5 PM, at midnight'. PYQ FREQUENCY: for/since distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Pick the correct: 'He arrived ___ the airport ___ time.'

options.option_text: at, in (at place, in time idiom)

questions.explanation: (1) 'AT THE AIRPORT' — 'at' for SPECIFIC LOCATION/POINT (airport, station, school, home, office, etc.). (2) 'IN TIME' is an IDIOM meaning 'before deadline' (e.g., he was on time AT or BEFORE expected time). PREPOSITIONS for PLACES: (a) AT: specific points (at the door, at the bus stop, at the cinema, at home). (b) IN: enclosed spaces or large areas (in a room, in India, in the box, in Mumbai). (c) ON: surfaces (on the table, on the wall, on the floor). PREPOSITIONS for TIME: (a) AT: specific time (at 5 PM, at midnight, at noon). (b) IN: months, years, parts of day (in March, in 2024, in the morning). (c) ON: days, dates (on Monday, on 5 January, on my birthday). IN-TIME vs ON-TIME (idioms — different meanings): (a) ON TIME = exactly at scheduled time, punctual. 'The train was on time.' (b) IN TIME = before deadline, not late. 'He arrived in time to catch the bus.' INDIAN ENGLISH usage may vary slightly; standard British/American English follows above patterns. PYQ FREQUENCY: at/in/on idioms in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose: 'She is angry ___ him ___ his behaviour.'
questions.explanation: EMOTION + PERSON + REASON construction: 'angry WITH (a person) FOR/ABOUT (a reason/thing)'. So 'angry WITH him FOR/ABOUT his behaviour'. Both 'for' and 'about' work; 'for' more common with concrete reasons. KEY EMOTION-PREPOSITION PAIRS (memorize): (1) ANGRY: with someone, at/about something. (2) AFRAID OF something/someone. (3) PROUD OF something/someone. (4) ASHAMED OF. (5) JEALOUS OF. (6) FOND OF. (7) SUSPICIOUS OF. (8) AWARE OF. (9) CAPABLE OF. (10) FAMOUS FOR. (11) RESPONSIBLE FOR. (12) GRATEFUL FOR. (13) SORRY FOR/ABOUT. (14) GOOD AT (skill). (15) INTERESTED IN. (16) CONFIDENT OF/IN. (17) WORRIED ABOUT. (18) ENTHUSIASTIC ABOUT. (19) TIRED OF. (20) BORED OF/WITH. ADJECTIVE-DEPENDENT PREPOSITION: many emotion-adjectives have FIXED prepositions; learn pairs by heart. EXAM TIP: when stuck, try inserting each preposition; the 'natural' choice is typically correct. SAMPLE: 'He is GOOD AT mathematics' (NOT 'in'). 'She is INTERESTED IN history' (NOT 'on'). 'The dog is AFRAID OF thunder' (NOT 'from'). PYQ FREQUENCY: adjective-preposition combinations in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Pick the correct: 'The book is divided ___ ten chapters.'
questions.explanation: 'DIVIDED INTO' is the standard collocation for SEPARATING something into PARTS/SECTIONS. 'Into' = movement INTO + becoming part of = SEPARATION result. KEY DISTINCTION: IN vs INTO: (1) IN — describes a STATIC LOCATION (where something IS): 'The book is IN the bag.' (2) INTO — describes ENTRY or TRANSFORMATION: 'He went INTO the room.' 'The water turned INTO ice.' PRACTICE: (1) 'The lecture was divided INTO three parts' (NOT 'in'). (2) 'Pour the water INTO the glass' (movement). (3) 'She broke the chocolate INTO 10 pieces.' (4) 'Translate this INTO Hindi' (transformation). VS IN — STATIC: 'I am IN the room.' 'The pen is IN my hand.' COMMON DIVIDED-INTO contexts: (a) Books/chapters: 'divided into chapters'. (b) Numbers: 'divide 100 INTO 4 equal groups = 25 each'. (c) Time periods: 'divided into seasons'. (d) Geographic regions: 'India is divided into 28 states'. EXAM TRAP: 'in' or 'into'? — if there's MOTION, BREAKING UP, or TRANSFORMATION: use 'into'. If static location: use 'in'. PYQ FREQUENCY: in/into distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose: 'I differ ___ you on this point.'
questions.explanation: BOTH 'differ FROM' AND 'differ WITH' are CORRECT but with DIFFERENT NUANCES: (1) DIFFER FROM = TO BE DIFFERENT (in nature, type, kind). 'Apples differ FROM oranges in taste.' (2) DIFFER WITH = TO DISAGREE (in opinion). 'I differ WITH you on this point' = I disagree with you. SAMPLE: 'My view differs WITH the popular opinion' (disagreement); 'Indian English differs FROM American English' (difference in form). VERB-PREPOSITION PAIRS to memorize: (1) DIFFER FROM/WITH (above). (2) AGREE WITH (a person) / TO (a proposal): 'I agree with you / I agree to your plan'. (3) ARGUE WITH (a person) / ABOUT (a topic). (4) APOLOGIZE TO (a person) / FOR (an act). (5) BORROW FROM (a person/place). (6) COMPARE TO/WITH: 'compare TO' (find similarities) / 'compare WITH' (find differences). (7) CONSIST OF (be made up of). (8) CONGRATULATE ON (an achievement). (9) DEPEND ON. (10) PREFER X TO Y. (11) REMIND OF / ABOUT. (12) REPLY TO. (13) SEARCH FOR. (14) THANK FOR. (15) WRITE TO (a person) / IN (a language). EXAM TIP: certain verbs have fixed prepositions; learn through usage. PYQ FREQUENCY: verb-preposition pairs in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Identify the correct: 'The cat jumped ___ the table.'
questions.explanation: 'ONTO' = movement to a SURFACE; SETTLES on top of. 'The cat jumped ONTO the table' = jumped + ended up on top. KEY DISTINCTION: ON vs ONTO: (1) ON — STATIC location on a surface. 'The book is ON the table.' (2) ONTO — MOTION leading TO the surface. 'He climbed ONTO the roof.' SIMILAR DIRECTIONAL PREPOSITIONS: (a) IN/INTO — 'water IN the glass' (static) vs 'pour water INTO glass' (motion). (b) OFF/OFF OF (US) — 'jumped OFF the chair'. (c) UP/UP TO — 'walk UP to me'. (d) DOWN/DOWN INTO — 'fell down into the well'. (e) ACROSS/THROUGH — 'walked across the bridge' vs 'walked through the tunnel'. (f) OVER/UNDER — 'jumped over the fence' vs 'crawled under the fence'. (g) AROUND — 'walked around the house'. STILL/MOVEMENT pattern: STATIC = simple preposition; MOTION = compound (often + 'to'). NUANCE: 'into', 'onto', 'upon' are all motion-emphasizing variants. UPON (formal/literary): 'climbed upon a hill'. INFORMAL: often just 'on'. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: a motion verb (jump, run, climb, walk, crawl) typically pairs with motion preposition (into, onto, up to). PYQ FREQUENCY: motion vs static prepositions in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Pick the correct: 'I have known him ___ a long time.'
questions.explanation: 'FOR a long time' — duration of relationship. Use FOR with TIME PERIODS (an hour, a day, a year, a long time, ages, a moment, a while, a fortnight). Use SINCE with STARTING POINTS (Monday, 1990, I was 5 years old, lunch). KEY: 'a long time' is a DURATION phrase, not a specific starting point — 'for' is correct. EXAMPLES: (1) 'He has been working here FOR 10 years.' (2) 'They've been married SINCE 2010.' (3) 'I haven't seen her FOR ages.' (4) 'I haven't seen her SINCE my last visit.' COMMON 'FOR' + DURATION expressions: for an hour, for ages, for a moment, for a while, for some time, for many years, for a fortnight, for the past month. COMMON 'SINCE' + STARTING POINT: since Monday, since 5 PM, since this morning, since last week, since 2020, since I started college, since lunch, since the meeting. ALSO USED: PRESENT PERFECT TENSE typically requires for/since: 'I HAVE LIVED here for 5 years' (still living) / 'I HAVE BEEN WAITING since 9' (still waiting). PAST SIMPLE doesn't typically use for/since for completed periods (use 'from-to'): 'I lived there FROM 2010 TO 2015.' PYQ FREQUENCY: for/since with present perfect in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per paper.
